title: Show grayscale pixels in an image

seo.metaTitle: Show Grayscale Pixels - Find The Gray Areas
seo.metaDescription: Mark every pixel of an image whose red, green and blue values match, so you can see which parts carry no color. Free, local, no upload.
seo.longDescription: Show grayscale pixels finds the pixels of an image where the red, green and blue values are the same — the pixels that carry no hue — and renders them as a mask. It is the fastest way to see why a picture that looks colored still has gray areas, or to check whether a logo is purely two-tone before you simplify it. A tolerance decides how close the three channels have to be to count as equal, which matters because compression often leaves small differences the eye ignores. Everything runs in your browser, so the image is never uploaded.
facts: Runs entirely in your browser: no upload, no server, no signup.
Marks pixels with equal red, green and blue values — the pixels with no hue.
Two views: a black and white mask, or a highlight over the original picture.
Tolerance at zero requires exactly equal channels; higher catches near-gray pixels.
Free with no daily limit, no watermark and no account, also for commercial use.
howTo: Drop the image into the source area, or pick a file from your device.
Choose the view: a black and white mask, or a highlight over the original picture.
Set the channel tolerance: zero requires exactly equal values, higher values catch near-gray pixels.
Set the highlight color and opacity, then download the mask if you need it.

faq.q: What does the tolerance setting do?
faq.a: It is how far the red, green and blue values of a pixel may differ and still count as gray. At zero only exactly equal values match; a higher value also catches pixels that look gray but were compressed with slightly different channels.

faq.q: Will the result tell me the image is grayscale?
faq.a: No, the mask shows where the gray pixels are, including when they are only a part of the picture. For a plain yes or no answer use the grayscale check on this site.

faq.q: Why do I see almost nothing with a high tolerance?
faq.a: A high tolerance matches nearly every pixel, including the colored ones, so the whole picture lights up. Lower the tolerance to isolate the parts that are really gray.
